title: May 2024 PCC elections — FPTP's quiet return
hook: The first PCC elections under First-Past-The-Post delivered Labour 26 of 41 commissioners on turnouts as low as 13% — and almost nobody noticed.
lede: Since 2012, Police and Crime Commissioners had been elected using the Supplementary Vote — a two-choice preferential system. The Elections Act 2022 scrapped SV in favour of FPTP. The first test was 2 May 2024. Labour swept, Conservatives held Home Counties strongholds, and Reform won its first PCC seat. The change in voting system was consequential; the public barely heard about it.
body_md:
**The old system and why it was changed.** Supplementary Vote let voters mark a first and second preference; if no candidate passed 50% on first preferences, all but the top two were eliminated and second-preference transfers counted. It was used for PCCs, the Mayor of London and metro mayors. In 2021 several SV elections produced winners who lost the first-round plurality but won on transfers — the Conservatives' 2022 Elections Act framed this as democratically illegitimate, and moved all mayoralties and PCC elections to FPTP. Critics (Electoral Reform Society, LSE Elections Unit) warned FPTP in a multi-party field would produce winners with 30-35% mandates.

**What happened on 2 May 2024.** Labour gained 10 PCC seats to hold 26 of the 37 PCC areas in England and Wales (plus directly-elected mayors performing PCC functions in a further four). Conservatives retained Kent, Essex, Surrey, West Mercia and a handful of others — 10 total, down from 20. Reform UK won in Lincolnshire (Marc Jones had held for Conservatives; Reform's Jonathan Evison took the seat) — their first PCC-type victory. Plaid Cymru, Lib Dems and Independents held the balance — including Gwent, Dyfed-Powys, North Wales, and three independents.

**Turnouts were lower than any comparable election.** Average PCC turnout 2 May 2024: around 19%, down from 33% in the last non-parallel election of 2021. Several areas recorded under 15% — Durham (14.1%), Cleveland (13.7%), Humberside (17.2%). The combination of an awkward spring timing, low salience, and the absence of a parallel general election (which had not yet been called — that came on 22 May, for 4 July) meant PCC contests were decided by a small, usually partisan, slice of the electorate.

**Mandates were correspondingly narrow.** Several winning PCCs took office with 30-35% of votes cast on 15% turnout — roughly 5% of the eligible electorate. Philosophically this has always been true of PCC elections; structurally FPTP makes it sharper because winners no longer need to appeal for second-preference transfers. The policy consequence: commissioners with smaller mandates setting police-and-crime plans that bind constabularies to four-year strategies.

**The policy agenda.** 2024-28 plans show a strong Labour emphasis on neighbourhood policing restoration (Starmer's manifesto pledge of 13,000 more neighbourhood officers), anti-social behaviour powers, and rape and serious sexual offence specialist units. Home Office's 2024-25 Police Settlement of £18.4bn (core funding plus precept) is the vehicle; PCCs set council-tax precepts within Treasury-set caps, and those caps rose £13/band-D in 2024-25 — the highest single-year increase since the office was created.

**Constitutional footnote.** The Home Office's 2024 Policing White Paper (delayed from 2022, now reshaped under Labour) is expected to propose PCC mergers in selected small force areas — Bedfordshire, Warwickshire, Cleveland were all mentioned in early drafts. If this happens, some FPTP winners of 2024 will find their offices abolished before their 4-year term ends. The democratic consequences of a voting-system change the public barely noticed will then become unmistakable.
